## Compute for the
Agent Economy
Omniverse Compute (OMC) is a decentralized physical infrastructure network (DePIN) that turns idle GPUs worldwide into a verifiable, trust-minimized compute grid for autonomous AI agents and AI teams — settled on BNB Chain, paid per job in crypto.
Each entry delivers 20 OMC in full at claim and carries a 0.01 BNB processing charge for that claim; the OMC token deploys at TGE on 1 January 2027.

Executive Summary

### Verifiable Compute for the Agent Era
AI demand has shifted from training to always-on inference — autonomous agents now burn tokens planning, calling tools and writing code. Centralized clouds answer with CapEx, quota walls and vendor lock-in. OMC answers with a verifiable, trust-minimized GPU grid that agents can pay for directly, per job, in crypto.

🖥️

#### Idle GPU Activation
Hundreds of thousands of consumer GPUs (RTX 4090/3090), data-center spare capacity and hardware formerly used for proof-of-work stay underutilized. OMC aggregates them with zero marginal onboarding cost.
DePIN
💸

#### Ultra-Low Gas & Scale
A dedicated BNB Chain L2 rollup for node heartbeats, task allocation and per-second / per-task micropayments is planned but not yet deployed — today these functions run on BNB Chain, with the L1 anchoring final settlement and disputes.
L2 Rollup
🛡️

#### Trustless Verification
Per-job verification policy: spot-check re-execution, optional 2–3 node redundancy, and hardware TEE for confidential workloads. Results are checked before payment, so requesters never have to trust the provider.
Verification policy

Target Audience

### Four Primary Client Segments

🤖

#### AI Startups
Inference, fine-tuning and batch jobs — without enterprise discounts or GPU quota walls.

🧩

#### DeAI Projects
Always-on autonomous agent inference and fine-tuning — paid per job, natively crypto, machine-to-machine.

🎬

#### 3D & VFX Studios
Unreal Engine 5, Blender batch rendering and Gaussian Splatting at extreme compute spikes.

🔌

#### GPU Providers
Plug idle hardware into the protocol and get paid in OMC for the verified compute you provide.

Architecture

### Three-Tier Network Stack

L1Settlement Layer
BNB Chain mainnet — OMC token issuance, staking smart contracts, DAO governance and final dispute arbitration.

L2Orchestration Layer
L2 Rollup (planned, not deployed) — high-frequency node heartbeats, task-allocation state mapping, state-channel settlements and low-cost micropayments. Until it ships, these functions run on BNB Chain.

GPUCompute Grid
Off-chain containerized grid — Docker/Kubernetes sandboxes with CUDA/ROCm acceleration, NVLink inter-GPU links and P2P data transport.

Workflow

### Task Distribution & Matching
Every job is scored and routed by a weighted bipartite matching engine.

1

#### Task Lockup
Requesters lock OMC fee tokens in the escrow contract before dispatch.

2

#### Smart Scheduling
Nodes matched by VRAM, TFLOPS, bandwidth, latency & reputation score.

3

#### Sandbox Execution
Jobs run in isolated containers; outputs verified redundantly & via ZK proofs.

Value Capture

### Token Utility & Deflationary Mechanics

💠

#### Compute Payment
Currency for inference, fine-tuning and 3D rendering jobs.

🔒

#### Node Staking
Collateral proportional to hardware tier before receiving jobs.

🗳️

#### DAO Governance
Vote on protocol parameters and treasury allocation.

🔥

#### Burn
50% of every 8% protocol fee is burned outright — 4% of settled volume. Slashing burns a further 20%.

AI Compute Station

### Buy compute. The seller's stake is the guarantee.

🧾

#### You set the ceiling
Quote a reference rate and the contract settles at or below it, refunding the difference. No published price list — the station shows the arithmetic, not an offer.

🔒

#### Stake is the collateral
A provider can only take the job if its staked OMC meets the hardware tier. The same stake pays you back if it fails to deliver.

⚖️

#### 48-hour dispute window
Verified results release payment automatically. Anything contested goes to the 48-hour window, and slashed collateral is split 50% to you, 30% to the treasury, 20% burned.

Security roadmap

#### Custody, access control and signature agility
Privileged contract roles move to a 3-of-5 multisig with a 48-hour timelock before mainnet, and an independent audit completes before launch. Off-chain service traffic signed by OMC already uses ML-DSA (FIPS 204) — the migration schedule is in the post-quantum roadmap.

#### 📋 Airdrop Rules
· Airdrop pool: 20,000,000 OMC (2% of max supply) = 1,000,000 entries × 20 OMC, each entry paid out in full at claim.
· Complete all 3 social tasks above to unlock participation; one wallet per participant.
· Per-wallet cap: 5 base entries = 100 OMC, plus up to 5 referral entries earned by inviting friends — 10 entries (200 OMC) at most.
· Daily cap: 1 entry per calendar day (resets at 00:00 UTC+8).
· Registering is free — an entry is a signature, not a transaction: no gas, no payment. Claiming is not free; see the claim fee below.
· Participation is open now: the page displays your accumulated amount and keeps your registered entries in this browser. The claim window opens at TGE (1 January 2027, UTC+8), together with mainnet and staking — the whole amount is withdrawable in one claim on this page and can be staked immediately.
· Sybil clusters, bot accounts and mass-created social accounts are disqualified; the team may reallocate the pool.
· Claim fee — read this before you rely on the balance above. This is an airdrop: the 20 OMC per entry is earned by doing the tasks, not bought, and no price was ever set for it. Claiming carries a 0.01 BNB processing fee per entry, not per transaction: a base claim of 5 entries costs 0.05 BNB (about $37 at $742/BNB) and a full 10-entry claim costs 0.10 BNB (~$74), paid to the treasury in the claim transaction and not returned; network gas (~0.0004 BNB) is on top. The fee is flat and per entry: it does not move with the OMC price and it is not a percentage of the airdrop — the same 0.01 BNB whether OMC trades at $0.01 or $1. A claim fee is ordinary on BSC, where the claimer already pays gas; ours is fixed, per entry, and published here rather than discovered at the wallet. The money funds development — audits, testnet incentives, RPC and indexer costs, the node client and the sub-sites (60%) — and team operations (40%). It exists because a free claim is farmed by wallets that will never run a GPU, and because this project is not running a private round. Each entry is delivered in full when you claim it — 20 OMC per entry means 20 OMC, no cliff, no vesting tail.

### What 20 OMC is actually for
The airdrop does not pay out cash — it hands out a share of a compute network. Here is what one entry, and a full claim, actually buys.
· A share, not an amount. One entry is 20 OMC — 0.000002% of the fixed 1,000,000,000 supply. A full claim of 10 entries is 200 OMC — 0.00002%.
· A down payment on a node. Receiving jobs requires a bond, and tier 1 is $250 for a consumer GPU (RTX 3090 / 4090 class). At the $0.371 reference price a full claim covers about 30% of that bond — 674 OMC — and the rest is bought on the market. That is the honest value of the airdrop: it is not pocket money, it is the difference between being interested in running a node and being 30% of the way to affording one.
· A claim on emissions. Staked OMC earns from what the network emits, and the rate is a division, not a promise: APR = min(100%, annual emission ÷ total staked). More stake means a lower rate for everyone, which is why no headline number is published.
· A vote, not a veto. In the transition stage holders vote on fees, audit rates, slashing sizes and treasury spending. The proposal threshold is 100,000 OMC, so a full claim casts a vote rather than setting the agenda.

What the rate looks like at different stake levels Total staked network-wide | Rate, year-one schedule (ceiling 100%)

10,000,000 OMC | 100% — the ceiling binds here
20,000,000 OMC | 50%
50,000,000 OMC | 20%
100,000,000 OMC | 10%
20% of the 65,500,000 OMC TGE float (13,100,000) | 76%

⚠️ The ceiling is not a promise. Emission is gated on fee revenue: daily = min(schedule ÷ 365, k × trailing 30-day fees ÷ 30), with k starting at 3. A network that has not yet earned fees emits nothing, so the real rate can be 0% regardless of the table above. That is the design — it is what keeps a token from inflating while nothing is being sold — but it also means nobody should claim a return they can point at before a single job has been paid for.

## OMC Airdrop Is Open
20,000,000 OMC across 1,000,000 slots of 20 OMC each. Free to join — no purchase, no presale. Claiming opens 1 January 2027.
Published 27 October 2026 · updated 30 October 2026

Omniverse Compute has opened its
community airdrop. 20,000,000 OMC — two percent of the fixed 1,000,000,000
supply — is reserved for 1,000,000 slots of 20 OMC each, distributed first
come, first served. Joining is free: three social actions, no payment, no token
purchase, no deposit. Claiming opens with mainnet on 1 January 2027, and each
entry carries a flat 0.01 BNB processing fee at that point.

### Key facts
Token | OMC — BEP-20 on BNB Smart Chain
Total pool | 20,000,000 OMC — 2% of a fixed 1,000,000,000 supply
Per entry | 20 OMC, delivered in full in the claim transaction
Slots | 1,000,000 — first come, first served, no lottery
Cost to join | Free — no purchase, no presale, no deposit
Entry cap | 5 base entries + up to 5 referral entries = 10 entries (200 OMC) per wallet
Daily limit | 1 entry per calendar day
Claim processing fee | 0.01 BNB per entry, not refunded (0.05 BNB for a base claim)
Registration | Open now — since 27 October 2026
Claim window | 1 January 2027 — 31 March 2027 (UTC+8)

### How to take part

- Follow @Omniverse_Depin on X.
- Retweet and comment on the pinned post. Both are verified on the airdrop page, not on X.
- Join the Telegram group.
- Connect a BNB Smart Chain wallet on omc.network/airdrop and register
up to 5 base entries. Registering is a signature, not a transaction — it costs no gas.
Each invited wallet that registers its first entry adds one entry, up to 5 more.

### What is free, and what the 0.01 BNB covers
Free is the whole participation layer. The three tasks
are ordinary social actions, registering is a wallet signature that costs no gas, and
no OMC is sold at any point — there is no presale, no private round, and nothing to buy
to become eligible.
The 0.01 BNB per entry is charged once, when you claim,
inside the claim transaction. It is a processing charge for that transaction in the way
the network charges gas, and it is deliberately not indexed to the token price: the same
0.01 BNB applies whether OMC trades at $0.01 or at $1. It is not refunded, because it
funds work that has already happened — 60% to ecosystem development (audits, testnet
incentives, RPC and indexer costs, the node client) and 40% to team operations. Every
one of the 20 OMC in an entry still arrives in full.
This is stated in the announcement rather than in a
footnote because the alternative — a number discovered at the wallet prompt — is how
airdrops earn a reputation they do not recover from.

### Timeline
27 October 2026 | Registration opens. Three social tasks, one wallet, no payment.
1 January 2027 | Mainnet and TGE. The claim window opens; the first entries are claimed.
31 March 2027 | Claim window closes. Unclaimed slots return to the protocol.

### The token behind it
OMC settles compute jobs on BNB Chain. The protocol fee is
8% of settled job volume, charged to the requester: 50% burned, 30% to staked nodes,
20% to the treasury. Supply is fixed at 1,000,000,000 with no inflation parameter, and
emission is gated by trailing 30-day fee revenue so issuance tracks real usage rather
than a calendar. Circulating supply at TGE is 65,500,000 OMC. The airdrop is the only
allocation delivered in full at claim; the lock-ups sit on the investor allocations.
Full detail: Tokenomics and
Whitepaper.

### What is not live yet
Stated plainly, because a launch post that omits this is
not worth reading: there is no mainnet deployment, no token contract, no audit, and no
exchange listing. Those arrive on 1 January 2027 or later. Today there is a public
testnet, a working node client, and a registration flow. Treat everything else as
scheduled, not shipped.

### Scam warning
No OMC token exists before TGE. Any contract, presale,
or "claim portal" naming OMC today is fraudulent, including any that asks you to send
BNB to a wallet for gas. The team will never ask for a seed phrase or a private key.
The only addresses that matter are published on omc.network and in the
repository.

### Where to check any number in this post

## Tokenomics: OMC Supply & Emission
URL: https://omc.network/tokenomics · lang: en

Tokenomics

## Tokenomics
1,000,000,000 OMC, fixed at deployment. Here is where every token sits, who can move it, and when.
🪙 Token OMC · BEP-20 🔥 Maximum supply 1,000,000,000 📈 At TGE 6.55% circulating ⛓ Chain BNB Chain

Every number on this page is a design target published in advance, not a promise of performance. Parameters marked proposed in the whitepaper are validated on the testnet and may change through governance before mainnet. Where a figure can be read directly from a contract, this page links to it so you can check it yourself rather than take our word for it.

### 1 · Supply
OMC is a BEP-20 token on BNB Chain with a fixed maximum supply of 1,000,000,000. There is no inflation parameter and no mechanism that can raise the cap.
Two mechanisms reduce supply. Nothing increases it:

- Fee burn. Every settled job pays an 8% protocol fee, charged to the requester on top of the provider's quoted price. 50% of that fee is destroyed by the contract at settlement, which reduces total supply directly. That is 4.0% of settled job volume — 4.4× the sink of the previous 3%/30% split, which destroyed 0.9% and could not offset emission at any volume a new network reaches.
- Fee share to stakers. 30% of the fee is distributed pro-rata to staked nodes. Unlike emissions this is revenue, not dilution, and it is the only staking yield that survives a falling token price.
- Slashing burn. 20% of any slashed stake is burned. See section 6.
The remaining 50% is split 30% to staked nodes pro-rata and 20% to the Treasury. The staker slice matters: paid only in emissions, a staker has no reason to hold beyond farming, which makes the position mercenary by construction. A share of fees is revenue, and it survives a falling token price.

### 2 · Distribution
The full 1,000,000,000 supply is allocated at deployment. Nothing is held back outside these seven categories.
Category | Share | Amount (OMC)

Compute mining and node rewards | 50% | 500,000,000
Ecosystem and grants | 15% | 150,000,000
Institutional investors | 10% | 100,000,000
Team and core contributors | 10% | 100,000,000
Private investors | 8% | 80,000,000
Treasury and liquidity | 5% | 50,000,000
Community airdrop | 2% | 20,000,000
Total | 100% | 1,000,000,000

The community airdrop is listed separately from the investor allocations on purpose: it is the one allocation with no round behind it — no price was set for it, and nobody bought into it. Entries are earned by doing the tasks, and claiming carries a 0.01 BNB claim fee per entry that is not refunded — 0.05 BNB for a base claim of five entries. It is a flat processing fee, charged per entry and independent of the token price; it funds development and operations, and the Airdrop page publishes the amount and the split.

### 3 · Circulating supply at TGE
About 65,500,000 OMC — 6.55% of maximum supply — enters circulation on day one (1 January 2027):
At TGE | Unlocked (OMC)

Treasury and liquidity — 50% of the allocation, for initial liquidity | 25,000,000
Community airdrop — delivered in full at claim | 20,000,000
Private investors — 10% of the allocation | 8,000,000
Ecosystem and grants — 5% of the allocation | 7,500,000
Institutional investors — 5% of the allocation | 5,000,000
Team and core contributors | 0
Compute mining and node rewards | 0
Circulating at TGE | 65,500,000

No team or core-contributor tokens unlock at TGE. That allocation is subject to a 12-month cliff and then vests monthly over 24 months, so it cannot reach the market before 2028. Node rewards likewise start at zero and are released only against verified work (section 5).
A public vesting dashboard is planned to show locked and unlocked balances for every category against the contract balance.

### 4 · Vesting and cliffs
Category | At TGE | Cliff | Then

Community airdrop | 100% | — | Paid in full at claim; 0.01 BNB per entry, not refundable
Treasury and liquidity | 50% | — | Remainder managed by the DAO Treasury
Private investors | 10% | 3 months | Monthly linear over 18 months
Institutional investors | 5% | 6 months | Monthly linear over 24 months
Ecosystem and grants | 5% | 6 months lock | Monthly linear over 36 months
Team and core contributors | 0% | 12 months | Monthly linear over 24 months
Compute mining and node rewards | 0% | — | Emission schedule, section 5

### 5 · Emission schedule for node rewards
The 500,000,000 OMC node-reward pool is 400,000,000 scheduled plus a 100,000,000 DAO reserve that cannot be minted before 2037 without a governance vote. The scheduled ceilings are 10,000,000 in year 1, 20,000,000 in year 2, 30,000,000 in year 3, 40,000,000 in year 4 and 50,000,000 a year from year 5 to year 10, released linearly by day within each year. They are ceilings, not entitlements.
The curve is deliberately back-loaded. A flat 50,000,000 OMC in year 1 is 76% of the entire TGE float (65,500,000 OMC), paid to a network with no paying demand yet — dilution against a use case that does not exist, and new tokens whose only buyer is a market maker. A halving curve errs the other way, spending three quarters of the pool inside four years. Starting at 10,000,000 cuts first-year dilution to 15% of float.
Emission is capped by revenue, not only by the calendar. The rate paid in any period is
min(annual ceiling / 365, k × trailing 30-day fee revenue / 30), with k decaying from
3 in year 1 to 0.5 from year 6. A schedule can only say how fast the pool may be
spent; the gate says how fast it is spent relative to what the network earns. No revenue means no emission, so a
network that never finds demand never inflates.
The consequence is the cleanest number on this page. Inside the gate both burn and emission are linear in fee
revenue, so their ratio is independent of volume and of price: 17% in year 1, 25% in year 2,
33%, 50%, 67%, and 100% from year 6 — at which point emission equals burn and circulating supply
stops growing at any scale. Above the gate, when the network is genuinely earning, the ceiling binds instead, and
because the burn keeps scaling with volume those years are deflationary. Unemitted amounts stay unminted; the pool
is not a promise to mint.

### 6 · Staking ladder and slashing
Nodes stake OMC before they may accept jobs. The required amount is a published five-rung ladder. Rungs are denominated in USD and restated into OMC at each re-peg, so the bond keeps its size while the token price moves. The amounts on the testnet are placeholders; /stake reads the live OMC figure from the contract.
Tier | Hardware class | Target bond (USD) | OMC on the testnet today

1 | Consumer GPU, up to 24 GB VRAM (RTX 3090 / 4090 class) | $250 | 20 (placeholder)
2 | Workstation / professional GPU (RTX A6000, L40S class) | $1,000 | 100 (placeholder)
3 | Data-centre GPU, 80 GB class (A100 / H100 single card) | $5,000 | 500 (placeholder)
4 | Multi-GPU data-centre node (2–8 accelerators) | $15,000 | 1,000 (placeholder)
5 | Cluster-scale deployment (multi-node) | $50,000 | 5,000 (placeholder)

The steps are non-linear by design: the rungs separate provider classes rather than pricing a small step up in hardware. Two problems in the old fixed-OMC ladder are worth stating, because both were arithmetic. First, 20 OMC per tier-1 machine was a $20 deposit behind a $1,500 GPU at a one-dollar token — a guarantee in wording only. Second, tier 1 was exactly one airdrop entry and tier 2 exactly one full airdrop, so a wallet could mint a stake out of nothing and draw emissions without ever buying OMC. USD pricing fixes the first outright and the second as a side effect: a maximum airdrop is 100 OMC, and turning that into a $250 tier-1 bond would need OMC at $2.50. Targets and the amounts last applied are recorded in contracts/params.json.
Slashing penalties, as a percentage of the stake:
Offence | Penalty

Job timeout | 2%
Unexpected offline during an active job | 5%
Incorrect output (failed verification) | 30%
Proven fraud or fake heartbeat | 100%

Slashed tokens are split 50% to compensate affected requesters, 30% to the DAO Treasury and 20% burned. The whole split is applied by the staking contract itself; the compute-market contract does not pay any of it a second time.

### 7 · The staking reward ceiling
Node rewards are emitted at a rate per second, and a fixed rate pays the same absolute amount however little is staked — which, over a nearly empty pool, would imply a meaningless annualised figure. The scope of that problem is bounded by arithmetic, not by policy: the staking contract clamps the rate it actually pays to a ceiling derived from the total amount staked, and both the ceiling and the rate in force are readable from the contract at any time.
Three properties matter, and all three are enforced on-chain:

- It is a maximum, not a promise. It bounds what a staker can be paid per unit of stake. It never raises that bound, and it never guarantees a payout.
- It needs no price oracle. Rewards and stake are denominated in the same token, so the bound is pure arithmetic and cannot be dodged by moving a price.
- It releases itself. While total stake is small the ceiling binds and the emission schedule is irrelevant; as stake grows the ceiling stops binding on its own and the schedule in section 5 takes over.
This site publishes no advertised rate of return, because none exists. Staking on OMC is a security deposit that can be partially or fully slashed, not a yield product. The live rate in force is shown on the Staking page, read from the contract.

### 8 · Contracts
The live contracts are on BNB Smart Chain Testnet (chainId 97). They are published here so that everything above can be checked against the chain rather than against this page.
Contract | Address

OMC token (tOMC) | 0xBEB21E40FB50A0F4ba9287C2058DC7851e450671
OMCStaking | 0xa70B8506a1a614Fd83D0C70d73Da1E21fdcf1fB6
OMCComputeMarket | 0x7664f1e73c2CBCbaFE636a653C173378C369C40A

These are testnet contracts and tOMC has no monetary value. It is not sold anywhere, it is not listed on any exchange, and it will not carry over to mainnet. Never send real funds to these addresses.

### 9 · Where to verify all of this

- Whitepaper section 7 — the authoritative text for payments, distribution, the emission schedule and slashing, on the Whitepaper page.
- Testnet page — RPC endpoints, deployment records and the node onboarding guide, at /testnet.
- Staking page — the ladder, the live emission rate in force and the exit procedure, at /stake.
- Repository — contract sources, deployment manifests and the automated security-testing evidence, at github.com/CBTdao/omc-network. The contracts have been through automated security testing, with an independent audit scheduled before mainnet — see SECURITY.md.

## Whitepaper v3.0
URL: https://omc.network/whitepaper · lang: en

Whitepaper · v3.0

## Omniverse Compute (OMC)
Decentralized GPU Computing Network — BNB Chain Ecosystem & Layer 2 Rollup Dedicated Scaling Network. Native Token: OMC (BEP-20).

📄 Whitepaper v3.0 (English)Full document · PDF · 21 pages 📊 Whitepaper DeckPresentation deck · PDF · 13 slides

### Contents
1 · Executive Summary 2 · Problem and Opportunity 3 · Supported Workloads and Limits 4 · Architecture 5 · Verification and Trust 6 · Security and Privacy 7 · Economics and the OMC Token 8 · Governance 9 · Competitive Landscape 10 · Roadmap 11 · Team, Audits and Legal 12 · Risk Factors 13 · References and Data Sources This document is provided for informational purposes only. It is not an offer to sell, or a solicitation of an offer to buy, any token or security, and it is not investment, legal, tax or accounting advice. OMC is a utility token intended for use within the OMC network; no return, price appreciation or liquidity is promised or implied. Statements about future development are forward-looking and may not be realized. The availability of the token may be restricted in some jurisdictions; it is the reader's responsibility to comply with local laws. Readers should review Section 12 (Risk Factors) and obtain independent professional advice before participating.

### 1 · Executive Summary
Omniverse Compute (OMC) is a decentralized physical infrastructure network (DePIN) that connects owners of idle GPU capacity with people who need compute — autonomous AI agents and AI teams, Web3 and decentralized-AI projects, and 3D and render studios. Providers earn OMC and fees by running verified jobs. Requesters get GPU capacity without cloud quotas, long-term contracts or vendor lock-in.
OMC is built on three ideas:

- Honest scope. OMC targets workloads that distribute well across independent machines: inference — including always-on agent inference — single-node fine-tuning, batch rendering and other embarrassingly parallel jobs. It does not claim to replace tightly coupled data-center clusters for frontier-scale model training.
- Verification you can price. Every job is covered by a verification policy chosen by job type, combining spot-check re-execution, optional full redundancy, hardware-based confidential computing where available, and economic penalties through staking and slashing.
- Token demand tied to usage. Fees are paid per job, a share of every fee is burned, and reward emissions are paid only against verified work.
Settlement and governance run on BNB Chain. High-frequency scheduling, heartbeats and micropayments are designed to run on a dedicated Layer 2 rollup built on the OP Stack (opBNB); that rollup is not deployed yet, so at testnet these functions run directly on BNB Smart Chain testnet. Jobs execute off-chain in sandboxed containers on provider hardware.

### 2 · Problem and Opportunity
Demand. The compute market has moved from training to inference. Autonomous agents now burn tokens continuously — planning, calling tools, writing code — and that demand is machine-paced, not human-paced. Small teams and independent developers still face high hourly prices, regional quota limits and dependence on a few cloud vendors. Render and simulation studios face sharp, short-lived peaks in demand.
Supply. Large amounts of capability sit underused: consumer and workstation GPUs, idle capacity in small data centers, and hardware formerly used for proof-of-work mining.
Gap. There is no widely trusted, agent-ready layer for strangers to rent GPU time with guarantees about correctness, data protection and payment — so autonomous agents still cannot buy compute from each other natively. OMC aims to provide that missing layer.

#### Target users
Segment | Typical workloads | What they need

AI startups and independent developers | Inference, LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning, batch embedding & vector jobs | Lower cost, no quota waits, simple APIs
Web3 and decentralized-AI projects | Agent inference, ZK proof generation | Crypto-native payment, censorship resistance
Rendering and 3D studios | Blender batch rendering, Unreal Engine offline rendering, 3D reconstruction | Burst capacity, per-job pricing
GPU owners and small data centers | Monetizing idle hardware | Predictable earnings, low operating friction

Cost position. We expect savings versus hyperscale on-demand pricing for suitable workloads, but we do not publish a fixed percentage until it is measured. Published benchmarks compare delivered cost per job, including verification overhead, against named alternatives. The benchmark methodology and the underlying rate data are published with the DCF forum GPU Pricing Watch series (see Section 13); the first delivered-cost report is published alongside the mainnet release.

### 3 · Supported Workloads and Limits
Workload class | Status | Notes

Batch rendering (Blender, UE offline) | Supported on testnet; mainnet rollout in Phase 2 | Deterministic seeds allow tolerance-based verification
Model inference | Supported on testnet; mainnet rollout in Phase 2 | Latency-sensitive jobs use region-aware scheduling
Single-node fine-tuning (LoRA/QLoRA) | Supported on testnet; mainnet rollout in Phase 2 | Job must fit within one node's VRAM
Multi-GPU jobs within one machine | Supported where the node has the required interconnect | Interconnect such as NVLink is a node attribute, declared and verified at registration
Multi-node distributed training over the public internet | Not supported | Bandwidth and latency make this impractical on consumer networks
Cluster jobs on co-located data-center nodes | Research track | Requires verified low-latency fabric between nodes

Consumer GPUs generally do not offer NVLink. OMC treats interconnect as a declared, tested hardware attribute and never assumes it.

### 4 · Architecture

#### 4.1 Layers
L1 settlement (BNB Chain). OMC token contract, staking contracts, DAO governance, and final dispute arbitration.
L2 rollup orchestration (planned, not deployed). Node heartbeats, job allocation records, state-channel settlement and micropayments are designed to run on an OP Stack rollup on BNB Chain (opBNB). On the testnet these functions are handled directly by the BNB Chain contracts. When the rollup launches it will start with a single sequencer operated by the project submitting batches to L1. The published path to decentralization covers rotating sequencer sets, and the rollup's data-availability layer, challenge window, withdrawal delay and user exit procedure will be documented in the technical documentation released with the rollup.
Off-chain compute grid. Provider nodes run jobs in isolated containers with CUDA or ROCm acceleration. Inputs and outputs move over encrypted peer-to-peer or relayed channels.

#### 4.2 Job Lifecycle

- The requester submits a job: container image, resource needs (VRAM, driver version, region), maximum price, verification policy and data-protection level.
- Escrow: the maximum price is locked in the L2 payment contract.
- The scheduler selects eligible nodes (Section 4.3).
- The node pulls the image, receives encrypted inputs, executes the job and returns outputs with an execution attestation.
- Verification runs according to the job's policy (Section 5).
- Settlement: if verification passes, the node is paid from escrow, the protocol fee is split (Section 7.1) and the node's reputation is updated. If it fails, the job is re-run on another node and the faulty node is penalized (Section 7.5).

#### 4.3 Scheduling
Scheduling has two stages.
Stage 1: hard filters. A node is eligible only if it meets the job's minimum VRAM, driver and CUDA/ROCm versions, region constraints, confidential-computing requirement if any, minimum stake and minimum reputation.
Stage 2: scoring. Each eligible node is scored on normalized metrics. Each metric is converted to a percentile rank (0 to 1) among eligible nodes for that job class, so that different units can be combined fairly:
Score = w_f × N(TFLOPS) + w_v × N(VRAM) + w_b × N(Bandwidth) + w_l × N(Latency, lower is better) + w_r × N(Reputation)
The weights sum to 1 and are set per job class. Proposed defaults:
Job class | TFLOPS | VRAM | Bandwidth | Latency | Reputation

Batch and rendering | 0.30 | 0.20 | 0.15 | 0.10 | 0.25
Inference | 0.20 | 0.15 | 0.10 | 0.30 | 0.25

Assignment is solved per scheduling window as a weighted matching problem that maximizes total score across all pending jobs and eligible nodes. To avoid concentrating work on a few top nodes, the final pick is drawn at random from the top-k scoring candidates. Weights and k are governance parameters.

### 5 · Verification and Trust
No single technique can verify every GPU workload, so OMC uses a policy selected per job.
Mechanism | How it works | Best for | Cost to requester

Spot-check re-execution | A random share of jobs (audit rate a) is silently re-run on an independent node and results are compared | All deterministic or near-deterministic jobs | Base price × (1 + a). Default a is proposed at 5% to 10%
Full redundancy | The job runs on 2 or 3 independent nodes and outputs are compared | High-value or high-precision jobs, chosen by the requester | 2× to 3×
Confidential computing (TEE) | Job runs inside a hardware-protected environment with remote attestation | Sensitive data or proprietary models; requires supporting GPUs | Premium for TEE-capable nodes
Zero-knowledge proofs | Cryptographic proof of execution | Research track; currently too costly for general GPU workloads | Not offered at launch

Handling non-determinism. GPU floating-point results can differ across devices and drivers. OMC therefore compares outputs using task-specific rules: exact hashes for deterministic jobs, numerical tolerance or perceptual metrics for rendering, and fixed seeds with deterministic kernels where inference supports it. Job types that cannot be verified reliably are labeled as such, and requesters are told before submitting.
Reputation. Each node has a score built from verified completions, uptime, timeouts and dispute outcomes. Scores decay without activity and cannot be transferred.
Disputes. A requester may dispute a result within 48 hours of the output being returned (proposed). The protocol first re-executes the job on an independent node. If the parties still disagree, the case escalates to L1 arbitration by a DAO-elected arbitrator set drawn from a pool of nine candidates, each posting a bond; a ruling is issued within seven days of escalation (proposed). Evidence (attestations, logs, hashes) is recorded on L2.

### 6 · Security and Privacy
Provider hardware is untrusted by default. OMC applies defense in depth, and is explicit about what it cannot guarantee.
Isolation. Jobs run in hardened sandboxes — gVisor by default, with higher-isolation tiers (Kata Containers or microVMs) selectable for sensitive workloads (proposed) — with no host access and no outbound network access by default.
Encryption. Inputs, outputs and images are encrypted in transit and at rest. Keys are released to a node only after it is assigned the job.
Data-protection levels. Standard (public or non-sensitive data), Protected (encrypted, ephemeral storage wiped after the job), and Confidential (TEE-only nodes).
Honest limitation. On non-TEE nodes, a malicious provider could in principle observe data or model weights in GPU memory. Requesters with proprietary models or regulated data should choose the Confidential level or not use the network.
Provider protection. Resource limits and abuse detection protect providers from malicious containers. Prohibited content and workloads are defined in the Acceptable Use Policy published on the official website.
Assurance. An independent security audit is planned before mainnet, and any report will be published when available (see Section 11). A bug bounty program is proposed to run from mainnet, paying severity-based rewards starting at $50,000 for critical findings on a public bounty platform (proposed). The contracts are currently self-reviewed on testnet — see SECURITY.md.

#### 6.1 Mainnet access control: multisig and timelock
Before mainnet, privileged contract roles — owner, verifier, market, treasury and the requester pool — will be held by a Gnosis Safe multisig rather than a single key, and sensitive operations (parameter changes, treasury withdrawals, role transfers and the emergency pause) will pass through a TimelockController so every change is publicly visible for a delay window before it executes. This is the part of the security story that is real today: it removes the single-key risk that most protocol losses actually come from — not exotic cryptography, but one compromised laptop or one leaked secret. The contracts already accept a plain address as the role holder, so this transition needs no ABI change. Live addresses and the signing threshold will be published in SECURITY.md once deployed.

#### 6.2 Post-quantum readiness (forward-looking)
OMC's post-quantum work starts on the layers it controls. Off-chain signatures issued by the project — the ai-tools service and claim authorizations — use ML-DSA (Dilithium, FIPS 204), with a working verification implementation in ai-tools-service/dilithium-poc. Contracts are upgradeable and follow BNB Chain as it adopts post-quantum signature standards; address-hygiene guidance is published for users. Token custody uses the base layer's ECDSA / secp256k1, the same assumption shared by BSC assets, and the migration timeline is tracked in docs/post-quantum-roadmap.md.

### 7 · Economics and the OMC Token
Parameters marked proposed in this section are design targets: they will be validated on testnet and may change through governance before mainnet.

#### 7.1 Payments and Fee Flows
Requesters pay per job in OMC or in supported stablecoins (USDT and USDC on BNB Chain). Paying in OMC receives a 10% fee discount. A protocol fee of 8% is charged to the requester on top of the provider's quoted price — not deducted from it, so a provider is paid what it quoted and the fee buys escrow, verification and dispute resolution rather than taxing the supply side. It is split as follows:

- 50% of the fee is destroyed by the smart contract at settlement. No market purchase is involved: jobs are escrowed and settled in OMC, so the fee is already denominated in the token, and burning it reduces total supply directly rather than routing it through an exchange.
- 30% is distributed pro-rata to staked nodes as a share of fees actually collected. This is the only yield in the system that is revenue rather than dilution, and it is why staking is a position rather than a farm.
- 20% goes to the Treasury for grants, audits and operations.
The burn equals 4.0% of settled job volume (8% × 50%). As an illustration only, not a forecast: if monthly settled volume were $10 million, the monthly fee burn would be about $400,000. Actual volume, and therefore burn, depends entirely on network usage. The protocol publishes settled volume, fees, burns and emissions on a public dashboard.
Why 8% and not 3%. At a 3% take with a 30% burn, the protocol destroyed 0.9% of volume. Offsetting the emission ceiling then required $33 million of annual settled volume in year one and $133 million by year five — figures no new compute network reaches, which made the burn decorative and the token structurally inflationary for its entire growth phase. At 8% and 50%, the sink is 4.4 times larger and the same break-even falls to $5.0 million and $25.0 million. The comparison to Web2 cloud still holds: a protocol take of 8% is a fraction of the 50-70% cost reduction the network delivers. The full arithmetic, including the scenario tables, is in ECONOMICS.md and reproducible with models/economics.mjs.

#### 7.2 Token Utility

- Payment for compute jobs, with a fee discount for settling in OMC (§7.6).
- Staking by node operators as security for honest behavior — the stake is simultaneously the right to accept work, the source of a buyer's refund and the discount qualification (§7.5, §7.6).
- Governance voting on protocol parameters, treasury use and upgrades.
- Rewards to providers for verified work.
OMC has a fixed maximum supply of 1,000,000,000 tokens on BNB Chain (BEP-20). The only mechanisms that reduce supply are the fee burn and the slashing burn. Both destroy tokens outright, so totalSupply() falls by the amount burned.

#### 7.3 Token Distribution
Category | Share | Amount (OMC) | Vesting

Compute mining and node rewards | 50% | 500,000,000 | 0% at TGE. Released over 10 years according to the emission schedule in 7.4
Institutional investors | 10% | 100,000,000 | 5% at TGE, 6-month cliff, then 24 months monthly linear
Private investors | 8% | 80,000,000 | 10% at TGE, 3-month cliff, then 18 months monthly linear
Community airdrop | 2% | 20,000,000 | 100% at claim — no cliff, no vesting tail
Ecosystem and grants | 15% | 150,000,000 | 5% at TGE, 6-month lock, then 36 months monthly linear
Team and core contributors | 10% | 100,000,000 | 0% at TGE, 12-month cliff, then 24 months monthly linear
Treasury and liquidity | 5% | 50,000,000 | 50% at TGE for initial liquidity; the remainder managed by the DAO Treasury

The airdrop is listed separately from investor allocations. Circulating supply at TGE is about 65.5 million OMC (6.55% of maximum supply): 20M of the airdrop (the pool is delivered in full at claim), 5M institutional, 8M private, 7.5M ecosystem and 25M treasury liquidity. A public vesting dashboard shows locked and unlocked balances for every category.
Why the claim pays in full. An entry is not a discount and not a reservation somebody else funded: it costs 0.01 BNB, it is not refundable, and the 20 OMC is what the participant receives for paying that and doing the tasks. Withholding 75% of it would mean advertising a number the claimer never sees on the day — the gap that turns a claim window into a complaint queue. What limits farming is the price and the caps, not a cliff: every wallet pays per entry, the per-wallet cap is ten entries, and the pool is first come, first served. The whole of the day-one pressure the airdrop can create is 20,000,000 OMC — 2% of supply — and every wallet that sells into it paid 0.01 BNB per entry for the position. The lock-ups sit where the discount is: private 10% at TGE then 18 months, institutional 5% then 24 months, ecosystem 5% then 36 months, and the team receives nothing for a year.
Airdrop mechanics. The 20,000,000 OMC airdrop pool is fixed and is paid out as 1,000,000 entries of 20 OMC each. Registration opens ahead of launch: the three social tasks can be completed and entries registered from the moment the campaign page goes live, because an entry is a reservation against the pool rather than a token — no OMC exists before mainnet. A participant can register up to 5 entries (100 OMC) through the campaign itself, plus up to 5 additional entries earned by inviting new participants — at most 10 entries (200 OMC) per wallet. Referral entries are drawn from that same fixed pool: the referral program changes how entries are distributed, never how many exist. A referral credit is granted only once the invited address completes its own first entry, and only for direct invites — the program is strictly single-layer, with no recursion, no downlines and no team commissions. Registering is free throughout: an entry is a signature, not a transaction, so there is no gas and no payment before the claim. Claiming is not free. The claim transaction carries a 0.01 BNB fee per entry (about $7.42 at the reference price of $742/BNB, so 0.05 BNB for a base claim of five entries and 0.1 BNB at the ten-entry cap) that the treasury keeps, split 60% to ecosystem development — audits, testnet incentives, RPC and indexer costs, the node client and the sub-sites — and 40% to team operations. It is charged for two stated reasons: a claim that costs nothing is farmed by wallets that will never run a GPU, and this project is not raising a private round, so the fee is how the remaining work is funded. The fee is a flat processing charge, not a price: it does not move with the OMC price and it is not set as a share of the airdrop's value, because the listing price is unknowable when the parameter is fixed. It is published with its dollar equivalent so that no one discovers it at the wallet. Each entry is delivered in full at claim: 20 OMC per entry means 20 OMC, with no cliff and no linear tail.
TGE, mainnet launch, staking and the airdrop claim window open on the same date (1 January 2027, UTC+8). Registration, by contrast, is open earlier, so the community is assembled before the token exists. Holding the claim to the TGE date is deliberate: the OMC a participant needs in order to stake is the OMC they accumulate during the campaign, and that OMC only comes into existence with mainnet. Entries become claimable the moment mainnet and staking open, so what a participant earns is stakeable from day one. A wallet that completes the campaign itself holds 100 OMC; a participant who also invites others can accumulate up to 200 OMC. Neither is enough to buy a staking bond at any price this token is likely to trade at, which is deliberate: the airdrop distributes a claim on the network, it does not fund a node. The claim window runs for three months and closes on 31 March 2027 (UTC+8).

#### 7.4 Emission Schedule for Node Rewards
The 500,000,000 OMC reward pool is 400,000,000 scheduled plus a 100,000,000 DAO reserve. The scheduled ceilings are 10,000,000 in year 1, 20,000,000 in year 2, 30,000,000 in year 3, 40,000,000 in year 4 and 50,000,000 a year from year 5 to year 10. Within a year, release is linear by day. The reserve cannot be minted before 2037-01-01 and requires a governance vote; it is not scheduled because scheduling it would have forced late-year ceilings up to 60,000,000 purely to make the arithmetic balance, which is the tail wagging the dog.
Those figures are ceilings, not entitlements. The binding constraint in most years is the revenue gate in §7.4.1, and whatever the gate withholds stays unminted rather than being deferred.
Year | Emission ceiling (OMC) | Share of pool

1 | 10.00M | 2.0%
2 | 20.00M | 4.0%
3 | 30.00M | 6.0%
4 | 40.00M | 8.0%
5 | 50.00M | 10.0%
6 | 50.00M | 10.0%
7 | 50.00M | 10.0%
8 | 50.00M | 10.0%
9 | 50.00M | 10.0%
10 | 50.00M | 10.0%
DAO reserve (unscheduled, 2037+) | 20.0%

The curve is deliberately back-loaded, and the reason is arithmetic rather than aesthetic. A flat 50,000,000 OMC in year 1 is 76% of the entire TGE float (65,500,000 OMC), handed to a network with no paying demand in its first year: dilution against a use case that does not exist yet. A halving curve errs the other way, spending three quarters of the pool inside four years. Starting at 10,000,000 cuts first-year dilution to 15% of float.

##### 7.4.1 The revenue gate
Emission is capped by revenue, not only by the calendar. The rate paid in any period is:
emission = min(annual ceiling / 365, k × trailing 30-day fee revenue / 30)
where k decays from 3 in year 1 to 0.5 from year 6. This single change fixes the property that made the previous design uninvestable: a schedule can only say how fast the pool may be spent, while the gate says how fast it is spent relative to what the network earns. No revenue means no emission, so a network that never finds demand never inflates — and an investor gets an answer to "when do you stop diluting me" that depends on an observable.
The consequence is the cleanest number in this paper. Inside the gate regime both burn and emission are linear in fee revenue, so their ratio is independent of GMV and of price:
Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6–10

Burn ÷ emission | 17% | 25% | 33% | 50% | 67% | 100%

From year 6 the ratio is 100% by construction: emission equals burn and circulating supply stops growing at any scale. Above the gate — when the network is genuinely earning — the ceiling binds instead, and because the burn keeps scaling with volume, those years are deflationary. The gate is applied by an EmissionController at mainnet that reads fee revenue from the settlement contract; on the testnet a keeper calls the owner setter monthly and every call is public. The APR ceiling in §7.5 remains as a backstop so a small stake base cannot be overpaid, but with the gate in place it is no longer meant to be the binding constraint.
Unemitted amounts are not deferred: whatever the gate withholds stays unminted, and the pool is not a promise to mint.

#### 7.5 Staking and Slashing
Nodes must stake OMC before receiving jobs. The required stake is a published ladder of five hardware tiers, each with its own minimum. Tier minimums are denominated in USD and restated into OMC at each re-peg, because a bond only deters if it is worth more than the damage an operator can do — and a fixed OMC figure stops being that the moment the token moves.
Tier | Hardware | Target bond (USD) | OMC on the testnet today

1 | Consumer GPU, up to 24 GB VRAM (RTX 3090 / 4090 class) | $250 | 20 (placeholder)
2 | Workstation / professional GPU (RTX A6000, L40S class) | $1,000 | 100 (placeholder)
3 | Data-center GPU, 80 GB class (A100 / H100 single card) | $5,000 | 500 (placeholder)
4 | Multi-GPU data-center node (2–8 accelerators) | $15,000 | 1,000 (placeholder)
5 | Cluster-scale deployment (multi-node) | $50,000 | 5,000 (placeholder)

The steps are deliberately non-linear, because the tiers separate provider classes rather than pricing a small step up in hardware: a node at tier 4 or 5 is underwriting data-center and cluster-scale capacity, and a proportionally larger slashing exposure.
Why USD, and what it fixes. The previous ladder was a fixed 20 / 100 / 500 / 1 000 / 5 000 OMC. Two problems, both arithmetic. First, at a one-dollar token that put a $20 deposit behind a $1,500 GPU and a job that could be worth more than both — the seller's stake was a guarantee in wording only, and the real verification pressure fell back on the protocol. Second, tier 1 was exactly one airdrop entry and tier 2 exactly one full airdrop, so a wallet could mint a stake out of nothing, collect emissions and never buy OMC. USD pricing closes the second one as a side effect: a maximum airdrop is 100 OMC, and reaching a $250 tier-1 bond with it would require OMC to trade at $2.50, so no separate lock is needed on airdropped tokens.
The OMC amounts currently on the testnet (20 / 100 / 500 / 1 000 / 5 000) are placeholders, not the ladder — tOMC has no price to anchor to, so there is nothing to restate against. The targets above are the published policy. At each re-peg the ladder is restated at the 30-day volume-weighted average price when that price leaves a ±25% band around the reference used at the previous restatement; contracts/params.json records both the targets and the amounts last applied, and contracts/tools/set-params.js is the only thing that writes them on chain. The OMC amount stored in the contract is authoritative: /stake reads it live from the contract and never caches a copy, so the page cannot drift from the chain.
Exit takes 14 days. A stake that can be withdrawn in the same block it was posted is a free option: stake, accrue emissions for a week, unstake, sell, repeat. The marginal participant is then a yield farmer rather than an operator, and the emission that was meant to buy capacity buys sell pressure. Withdrawal is therefore a two-step request: the node signals exit, keeps earning nothing and stays fully slashable for a 14-day cooldown, and only then can it withdraw. Fourteen days is long enough that farming carries real risk and short enough that an honest operator is not locked out of reselling hardware.
Slashing triggers and proposed penalties (percent of stake):
Offense | Penalty

Job timeout | 2%
Unexpected offline during an active job | 5%
Incorrect output (failed verification) | 30%
Proven fraud or fake heartbeat | 100%

Slashed tokens are allocated 50% to compensate affected requesters, 30% to the DAO Treasury and 20% burned (Burn = Slashed × 20%). Penalty sizes will be calibrated on testnet and published before mainnet.
Staking rewards carry a published ceiling. Reward emission is a rate per second (§7.4), and a fixed rate pays the same absolute amount however little is staked. A nearly empty pool would therefore imply a meaningless annualised return. The contract clamps what it actually pays:
> rate in force = min( emissionPerSecond , total staked × maxAprBps ÷ 10,000 ÷ 365 days )
maxAprBps is a contract parameter, and the contract itself bounds it to a maximum of 10,000 basis points — 100% per year. The current testnet deployment is configured at 2,000 basis points (20% per year); the value in force is readable from the contract and may be changed within the 10,000 bps bound. Three properties matter. First, the ceiling is enforced by the contract, not by policy: both the ceiling and the rate in force are readable from it at any time. Second, it needs no price oracle, because rewards and stake are denominated in the same token, so the bound is arithmetic and cannot be dodged by moving the price. Third, it is a maximum, not a promise — it bounds what a staker can be paid per unit of stake and never raises it. While stake is small the ceiling binds and the flat schedule is irrelevant; as stake grows the ceiling stops binding on its own and the schedule in §7.4 takes over. With the parameter in force the crossover sits at roughly 315,360 OMC staked across the network.

#### 7.6 The Compute Market: What the Stake Is Actually For
Staking only has meaning if the stake is doing work. In OMC it performs three concrete jobs, all of them enforced by a contract rather than by policy. The mechanism is the Compute Market — the buyer-facing half of the network. Suppliers register GPUs and stake; buyers post jobs and escrow payment. The market contract sits between them.
1. The stake is the right to accept work. A provider cannot be assigned a job unless its staked balance clears the hardware tier that job requires. The check reads the same ladder defined in §7.5 — the market contract does not keep its own copy. There is no separate reputation score gating assignment: eligibility is stake, and it is verified on chain at the moment of assignment. Below the tier minimum, the assignment reverts.
2. The stake is the source of the buyer's refund. When a job is created the payment is escrowed, not transferred. Settlement releases it only against an accepted result, and the contract settles at or below the buyer's stated ceiling, returning the difference. If a provider fails — missing the deadline, dropping offline mid-job, delivering output that fails verification — the penalty is taken from that provider's stake, never from another user's escrow, and the majority share is paid directly to the buyer. A refund is the seller's debt, not a redistribution of someone else's deposit. This is the property that makes the escrow trustworthy: the money that can pay the buyer back is locked before the job starts.
3. The stake earns a settlement discount. A buyer paying in OMC rather than a stablecoin receives a reduction on the protocol fee described in §7.1. The discount is a governance parameter, not a return: it changes what a buyer pays, not what a staker earns. It is deliberately modest, because an aggressive discount would convert a security deposit into a yield product and attract capital with no intention of running hardware.
Job lifecycle. A job moves through a fixed state machine: escrowed → assigned → delivered → settled, with disputed, refunded and cancelled as terminal branches. The buyer may cancel an unassigned job and recover the escrow in full. Once a result is delivered, the buyer has a 48-hour dispute window (§5) to contest it; uncontested results release automatically, so payment cannot be stalled indefinitely by buyer inaction.
Verification policy is chosen per job. Buyers pick the assurance level their workload justifies — spot-check re-execution of a sample, full redundant execution across independent nodes, or hardware attestation (TEE) — and the cost scales with it. This keeps cheap, low-risk jobs cheap rather than forcing every buyer to pay for redundant execution they do not need.
Scope at launch. The market is a testnet tool. It does not sell production compute and publishes no price list or rate; buyers quote their own ceiling and the arithmetic is shown, not an offer. Mainnet deployment follows the same schedule as staking (§10).

### 8 · Governance
Governance moves from team-led to community-led in stages.
Launch stage. Protocol upgrades are controlled by a 4-of-7 multisignature wallet held by core contributors, with a 3-day timelock (proposed). All changes are announced publicly before execution. Individual signers are not disclosed at this stage; the signing policy, key-management practice and any signer rotation will be published before mainnet.
Transition stage. OMC holders vote on parameters (scheduling weights, audit rates, fee split, slashing sizes, emission scaling) and Treasury spending. Proposed thresholds: a proposal threshold of 100,000 OMC, a quorum of 10% of circulating supply, a 7-day voting period and a 2-day execution delay.
Full DAO stage (2027 or later). The multisig is removed or limited to emergency security actions with transparent, time-limited powers.
Treasury reports are published quarterly.

### 9 · Competitive Landscape
OMC competes with centralized hyperscale clouds, centralized GPU marketplaces, and other decentralized compute networks. Sources and dates for every figure are listed in Section 13.
Dimension | Hyperscale cloud | GPU marketplaces | Other decentralized networks | OMC

Price per GPU-hour (H100 SXM, on-demand, Aug–Oct 2026) | $6.88–$12.29 | $2.49–$6.16 (Lambda, RunPod, Vultr, CoreWeave) | $1.25–$3.00 (Akash, io.net, Render) | Target: below marketplace median; measured benchmark to be published (§2)
Verification of results | Provider trust | Platform trust | On-chain attestation (Akash); Proof-of-Render and node tiers (Render); proof-of-time-difference and hardware scans (io.net) | Tiered policy per job, see Section 5
Confidential computing | Confidential VMs available; H100 CC on selected instances | Limited | Limited / varies by network | Optional TEE tier
Payment | Fiat | Fiat and crypto | Native token (AKT / IO / RENDER) | OMC and stablecoins
Supported workloads | Broad, including multi-node training | Broad, including multi-node clusters | Mainly single-node inference, fine-tuning and rendering; multi-node training is impractical | See Section 3

Hyperscaler figures are per-GPU-hour for H100 SXM5 80GB in 8-GPU instances (AWS p5.48xlarge $6.88; Google Cloud a3-highgpu-8g $11.06; Azure ND96isr H100 v5 $12.29), spot/preemptible runs $1.95–$2.80, with 1-year commitments around −30% to −38% and 3-year around −50% to −62% (vendor published pricing pages, observed September 2026 and cross-checked against independent trackers). Decentralized network figures are ranges published across 2026 sources (decentralised.news, 2026; gpumarketdepin.com, 2026) and vary by supply and workload class. Network uptime reported for decentralized networks (Akash 99.4%, Render 99.8%, io.net 98.6%) remains below hyperscaler SLAs (99.9%–99.99%).
The characteristics OMC intends to differentiate on — verification policy by job type, a published hardware-tier staking ladder, utilization-linked emissions and BNB Chain ecosystem integration — are stated here as design commitments; measured evidence will be published as the network runs.

### 11 · Team, Audits and Legal
Core team and advisors. OMC is developed by a pseudonymous collective of core contributors. Consistent with that practice, the project does not publish individual names, employment histories or personal profiles at this stage, and no advisory board is disclosed. All code contributions are public and attributable to the contributing accounts in the repository. If named advisors are engaged, their roles and the scope of their engagement will be published in this section.
Legal entity and jurisdiction. The network and the token are operated as an open-source project. The legal entity that will issue and hold the token, its registration details and the jurisdiction governing the token will be published in this section and on the official website before the token generation event. Until that disclosure is made, no other statement of entity or jurisdiction should be relied upon.
Funding. No external financing has been raised to date; development has been funded by contributor resources. If financing is raised, the amount, the investors and any terms that affect token holders will be disclosed here.
Smart contract audits. Independent audits of the smart contracts and the node client will be completed before mainnet launch. The full reports — auditor, scope, date and the status of every finding — will be published in this section.

### 12 · Risk Factors
Technical risk. Verification methods may fail on some workloads, smart contracts may contain bugs despite audits, and the L2 rollup may have availability or security issues.
Security and privacy risk. Non-TEE nodes cannot fully protect data in use. Sandbox escapes and side-channel attacks are possible.
Market risk. Token prices can be extremely volatile and may fall to zero. Liquidity may be thin. Unlock events may add selling pressure.
Adoption risk. The network needs enough requesters and providers. If demand is low, reward emissions are not matched by fee revenue and the burn is small.
Competition risk. Established clouds and other decentralized networks may offer lower prices or better reliability.
Hardware and supply risk. GPU prices, availability, export controls or energy costs may affect the provider base.
Regulatory risk. Laws on tokens, data protection and cross-border services may change and may restrict use in some countries.
Governance risk. Voting power may concentrate, and early-stage control by a multisig carries key-management risk.
Dependency risk. OMC depends on BNB Chain and third-party infrastructure.

### 2 · Register the node
Registering publishes your endpoint and starts the liveness clock. Registration is also the first heartbeat.
Node endpoint A reachable address that identifies this node. During the testnet the verifier only checks that it responds — it does not grade your hardware.

- Have a server? Use its public address, e.g. http://203.0.113.10:9190 or https://node.yourdomain.com
- No server? A GitHub Pages site, a gist, or any static page you control also works — the field only has to stay reachable.
- Just trying the flow? Any placeholder such as https://example.com registers fine — swap in a real address before you rely on it.
The verifier requests this address to decide whether the node is online. If it stays unreachable past the grace period, slashing starts.

### 3 · Reduce or exit
A registered node must stay at or above its tier minimum. To withdraw everything, deregister first — that drops the write requirement.

Mechanics

### What is actually enforced on-chain
Not a roadmap promise — these are the rules compiled into the deployed contract, each one exercised by the deploy script before handover.

🔒

### Tier minimums
Stake below the tier minimum and the transaction reverts. Withdrawing drops you to tier 0 the moment you fall under it.
min = base × tier
💓

### Liveness clock
Each heartbeat buys a fixed window. Miss it, and anyone — not just the team — can permissionlessly trigger the slash.
30 min + 10 min grace
✂️

### Slashing split
Each overdue interval burns 5% of the node's stake: 50% to requesters, 30% to the treasury, 20% permanently burned.
50 / 30 / 20
⛽

### Principal is untouchable
Rewards are paid only from the pre-funded reward pool. The contract never pays a reward out of somebody else's stake.
accRewardPerShare

Why slashing matters here. A staking token that cannot be lost is not a security deposit, it is a loyalty badge. The testnet runs the real penalty path — including a genuine, waited-out slash — so that the mainnet parameters are tuned against observed behaviour rather than a spreadsheet.

Safety

### How to read this page without trusting it

🧾

### Verify the address
Both contract addresses are on BscScan. The page reads the same public RPC your wallet does — nothing is proxied through a server we control.

🔑

### No approval for anything else
"Approve" writes an allowance for exactly the amount you are staking that moment — never an unlimited allowance.

🧪

### Wrong-chain guard
If your wallet is not on chain 97, the page asks to switch — or to add BNB Smart Chain Testnet — before anything is signed.

A stake that does something

### Staking is not a yield product. It is a three-part job.

🎟️

### It buys you the right to take work
The AI Compute Station only assigns a job to a provider whose stake clears the hardware tier. Below the minimum, the assignment reverts — that check is on chain, not in a UI.

💸

### It is where the buyer's refund comes from
If a provider misses a deadline, goes offline or returns a bad result, the penalty is taken from that provider's stake and 50% of it goes straight to the buyer. A refund is the seller's debt, not another customer's deposit.

🏷️

### It earns you a fee discount
Pay for compute in OMC instead of a stablecoin and the 8% protocol fee is cut to 7.2%. The discount is a policy parameter, not a promise of profit.

Read this before you stake. Staked tOMC is testnet-only and worth nothing. There is no advertised rate of return anywhere on this site, because none exists — releasing a handshake, missing a heartbeat, or delivering a result that fails verification all cost you real collateral. See the buyer side →

Lifecycle

### What happens after you click escrow
The same eight steps the whitepaper describes from the requester's side, with the part each contract plays marked.

1SubmitContainer image, resources, region, ceiling price, verification policy and protection level.

2EscrowThe ceiling is locked in OMCComputeMarket. It can never be charged more than this.

3FilterNodes that miss the VRAM, driver, region, TEE, stake or reputation bar are dropped.

4ScoreSurvivors are ranked on TFLOPS, VRAM, bandwidth, latency and reputation, weighted per job class.

5AssignA provider is drawn from the top-k and recorded on chain — the eligibility check runs in that transaction.

6ExecuteThe node pulls the image, gets the keys after assignment, runs the job and returns an attestation.

7VerifySpot-check, redundancy or TEE attestation decides whether the output is accepted.

8SettlePass: the provider is paid, the fee splits, reputation updates. Fail: bond slashed, requester refunded.

The part that is honest. The GPU runs off chain and the scheduler is a trusted role during the testnet, exactly as the verifier is on the staking contract. What is enforced on chain is the escrow, the eligibility filter, the settlement and the penalty. Disputes open for 48 hours after delivery; the protocol first re-executes the job on an independent node before anything escalates.

Pricing

### How the price is built — and what we will not claim

🧮

### Structure, not a rate card
GPU-hours × reference rate × verification multiplier, plus an 8% protocol fee, minus 10% of that fee when you pay in OMC. You set the ceiling; the contract refuses to settle above it.

🔍

### Verification is the price lever
Spot-check adds the audit rate on top. Full redundancy costs 2–3× because the work is done 2–3 times. TEE carries a premium and needs TEE-capable nodes to be online.

📉

### The target, stated plainly
OMC targets below the median of the centralized GPU marketplaces. Hyperscalers ran $6.88–$12.29 per H100 SXM GPU-hour, marketplaces $2.49–$6.16, other decentralized networks $1.25–$3.00. The measured OMC benchmark is published after mainnet.

No number on this page is a quote. The station shows the arithmetic and the target; it does not publish a price. Any figure you enter is your own ceiling. Treat every output of the box above as indicative — it is a way to see where the money goes, not an offer.

- 🔑 Browser wallets MetaMask, Trust Wallet and any other EIP-1193 provider

FAQ

### Testnet Questions

#### Do testnet rewards convert to mainnet OMC?
Testnet tOMC has no value. However, compute contributions and reputation scores accumulated on the testnet are tracked for the Compute Mining & Node Rewards pool (50% of supply) at mainnet launch.

#### What hardware do I need?
Any CUDA or ROCm GPU works on the testnet. Score weighting favors TFLOPS and VRAM — RTX 3090/4090 class cards land in the top hardware tiers, and NVLink-connected rigs get priority for multi-GPU jobs.

#### Is my data private?
Jobs run in hardened sandboxes (gVisor by default) with no host access. Results are checked under a per-job verification policy — spot-check re-execution, 2–3 node redundancy, or hardware TEE.

### Not a GPU owner? Still early.
Claim your community airdrop allocation — 2% of total supply, paid out in full when you claim.

## Upscale 4×.
Nothing Leaves Your Browser.
Real-ESRGAN runs inside this page. The model is downloaded once, then every image is processed by your own GPU or CPU — no server, no upload, no account, no wallet. This is the free tier of the OMC compute network: the same class of work the paid network settles on chain.
Inference happens on your device No payment, no signup

How this is honest. This page does not talk to the OMC network at all — there is no chain call, no escrow and no token involved. It is a plain client-side tool that happens to use the same model family the paid network runs. If you want the checkout, job records and provider collateral, that lives on the Compute Station.
Local only Your image is read into this tab and never uploaded. The only network request this page makes is the one-time download of the model file and the inference runtime.

### 1 · Pick an image
The model is 64 MB and is fetched once, then cached by the browser. Nothing runs until you ask it to.
Click to choose or drop an image here
PNG or JPG. Keep the long edge under 4096 px — a 4× result is 16× the pixels and a large photo will take minutes.

Tile size 128 — lowest memory, slowest 256 — recommended 384 — faster, needs more memory

A big image is cut into tiles, upscaled one at a time and blended back with overlap. Tiles are why a modest device can still finish a large picture — they trade speed for memory.

Original
Real-ESRGAN 4×

### What is actually happening
No black box — here is the whole pipeline, in order.
1 The model loads into this tab A 64 MB Real-ESRGAN export is fetched once and handed to ONNX Runtime compiled to WebAssembly. It is then cached, so a second visit does not download it again.

2 Your image is decoded and cut into tiles The file is drawn to a canvas, sliced into overlapping tiles and normalised to the float range the network expects. This all happens in memory inside the page.

3 Tiles are blended back into one picture Each tile is upscaled 4×, the overlap is cropped off, and neighbouring tiles are averaged so the seams do not show. Then you get a download button.

### Why speed depends on your device
The same model runs on a phone and on a desktop GPU, and the difference is large. These are measured reference points, not promises about your machine.
Input | Output | Reference time

320 × 200 | 1280 × 800 | ~2 s
640 × 400 | 2560 × 1600 | ~8 s
1024 × 640 | 4096 × 2560 | ~23 s

Measured on a modest dedicated GPU. Integrated graphics and phones will be slower — often several times slower. A 12-megapixel phone photo is not a realistic input for this page; crop it first.

### Free here, settled on chain there
Two different things, deliberately kept apart.
A This page — free, no wallet A convenience tool. Your device pays the compute cost in electricity and time. There is no job record and nothing to settle.

B The network — paid, on chain When you need a guaranteed run on someone else's GPU with verifiable output and a refund if it fails, that is a job on the Compute Station, settled in tOMC on BNB Smart Chain Testnet.

Need a guaranteed run, not a free tool? Open the Compute Station. →

Model and licence. Real-ESRGAN x4plus (RRDBNet, 23 blocks), exported to ONNX without weight changes. Licensed BSD-3-Clause, which permits commercial use. This page runs it unmodified; it is the same model family the paid network is benchmarked with.

On chain

### Send this job to the network instead
The tool above spends your own device. This block spends tOMC: the escrow, the provider assignment, the delivery hash and the settlement are all recorded on BNB Smart Chain Testnet and can be checked in the explorer without trusting this page.

What is on chain, and what is not On chain: the escrow, which provider was assigned, the keccak256 of the result, the settlement and any slashing — all readable with one getJob(jobId) call. Not on chain: the image itself. No EVM can hold a megabyte of pixels, so the bytes travel out of band and the chain carries only their hash. Right now no provider process is serving testnet jobs, so a job you create will be escrowed and stay in ESCROWED until one is. The escrow is real and refundable through cancelJob; the transport is the piece still being built.

Boundaries

### What this tool will and will not do

🔒

### It will not upload your image
There is no upload endpoint. The runtime and the model file are the only things fetched from the network, and both are static assets. You can watch the network tab and see for yourself.

🐢

### It will not be fast on weak hardware
Speed is a property of your device, not of the page. If you are on integrated graphics, start with a small image and expect to wait. There is no server-side fallback here by design.

🧾

### It will not pretend to be the network
No wallet, no token, no fake job counter. It is a tool, labelled as a tool. The chain-backed service is a separate page with its own escrow, verification and penalties.

Why build the free tool first. The network's honest weakness is that it has no jobs yet. A tool that is useful on its own — even with the chain switched off — earns attention before it asks anyone to trust a marketplace. This page is that first step; the paid side is built to be earned, not assumed.

### Supported wallets
Any EIP-1193 wallet works. Inside the Binance App this dApp connects through the Binance Web3 Wallet that Binance injects at window.binancew3w.ethereum — not at window.ethereum.

- Binance Web3 Wallet Detected automatically inside the Binance App — no extension needed
- 🔑 Browser wallets MetaMask, Trust Wallet and any other EIP-1193 provider
- ⛓ Network BNB Smart Chain Testnet (chainId 97) — the page requests the switch for you
The Binance Web3 Wallet lives inside the Binance App, not as a browser extension. This reopens the current page there, on BNB Smart Chain Testnet.
