Reference data

### Published on-demand list prices
USD per GPU-hour. Hyperscaler figures are 8-GPU node prices divided by eight; Lambda and CoreWeave are quoted per GPU or per node as noted.

GPU | AWS | Google Cloud | Azure | Lambda | CoreWeave

H100 80GBSXM5 · node spec in notes | $6.88p5.48xlarge · $55.04 ÷ 8 | $11.06a3-highgpu-8g · $88.49 ÷ 8 | $12.29ND96isr H100 v5 · $98.32 ÷ 8 | $3.99per GPU, on demand | $6.16HGX H100 · $49.24 ÷ 8
H200 141GBSXM · node spec in notes | $7.91p5en.48xlarge · $63.30 ÷ 8 | $10.60a3-ultragpu-8g · $84.81 ÷ 8 | $13.78ND96isr H200 v5 · $110.24 ÷ 8 | — | $6.31HGX H200 · $50.44 ÷ 8

On-demand list prices as published by each vendor, observed September 2026 in US regions (AWS us-east-1, Google Cloud us-central1, Azure East US). Excludes tax, storage, networking and support. Spot, preemptible and committed-use prices are lower — Google, for example, prices H200 below H100, so read the row, not the generation. Rates change often: confirm current pricing with the vendor before relying on any figure here. Sources: AWS EC2 on-demand pricing, Google Cloud accelerator-optimized pricing, Azure Retail Prices API, Lambda and CoreWeave public pricing pages.

Total cost of ownership

### What the hourly rate leaves out
Three cost mechanisms most price tables ignore, and which decide the real bill far more than the headline rate.

⏱️

#### Idle hours are billed
A p5.48xlarge bills $55.04 per hour whether its eight GPUs are training or doing nothing — roughly $4,000 over a single long weekend. On-demand pricing charges for wall-clock time, not for work delivered.
Wall-clock billing
📡

#### Egress sits on another page
Outbound data is priced separately: about $0.09/GB on AWS, $0.08/GB on Azure and $0.08–0.12/GB on Google Cloud. For a mid-sized H100 deployment moving checkpoints and outputs, that commonly adds four figures a month.
Data transfer
🔒

#### Discounts do not cover the GPUs
The capacity AI teams actually buy is often excluded from the discounts designed to save money: AWS Spot is outside Savings Plans, Capacity Blocks are outside both Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, and Google excludes A3/A4 from flexible committed-use discounts.
Commitment structure

Design intent

### How OMC's model is designed to differ
A comparison of billing mechanics, not prices. OMC has published no network rates; the items below are design commitments from the whitepaper and may change before mainnet.

Dimension | Hyperscaler on-demand | OMC (designed)

Billing unit | Per hour, whole instance | Per job, with per-second micropayments on the L2 rollup (planned; today settlement is on BNB Chain)
Idle time | Running hours are billed | Intended to settle only for accepted, verified work
Capacity access | Regional quota limits and availability gates | Permissionless, subject to supply on the network
Commitment | None required; discounts need 1–3 year commitments | No commitment required by design
Payment | Fiat, via vendor billing | OMC or supported stablecoins (USDT / USDC on BNB Chain)
Result verification | Provider trust | Tiered verification policy per job type (spot-check re-execution, redundancy, TEE)

Design commitments reflect OMC whitepaper v3.0 and are stated as intent, not as shipped functionality. OMC is in testnet; mainnet opens on 1 January 2027. Nothing here is a price commitment, a service-level commitment or an offer to sell compute.
Comparing against a real purchase? This page compares list prices. The AI Compute Station is the buyer-facing side of the network — it lets you quote a job and escrow against it, with the provider's staked OMC standing behind delivery. It is a testnet tool; it does not sell compute and publishes no rates.

Questions

### Frequently asked questions

Why is there no OMC price in the calculator? Because there is no published OMC network rate to quote. The mainnet opens on 1 January 2027, and until rates are set and published, any figure we printed would be an invention. Instead the calculator lets you type your own hypothetical rate and shows you the arithmetic — clearly labelled as your assumption, not our price.
What exactly does "per GPU-hour" mean in the table? Hyperscalers sell GPU capacity inside fixed machine shapes. AWS p5.48xlarge, Google's a3-highgpu-8g and Azure's ND96isr H100 v5 each bundle eight H100 GPUs, so the honest comparable number is the node price divided by eight. Comparing a per-node price against a per-GPU price is the single most common way GPU price tables mislead — a headline "$49.24" can be more expensive per GPU than a "$3.99" once the unit is aligned.
Do these figures include storage, networking and support? No. They are compute list prices only. Storage, egress, load balancers, snapshots and any support tier sit on top, and for sustained deployments those lines are material — egress alone commonly adds four figures a month for a mid-sized training cluster.
Why not show spot, reserved or committed-use rates? Spot and committed rates are real and often far lower, but they are not like-for-like: spot capacity can be reclaimed, and committed-use discounts require one- to three-year commitments and often exclude the newest GPU families. Mixing them into one table is how "cheapest" claims get made. This page sticks to on-demand list prices, which are the only rates that are both published and directly comparable.
How current is this data, and how often is it updated? The rates were observed in September 2026 from vendor pricing pages. GPU pricing changes frequently, so we date every figure rather than presenting it as permanent. Treat this as a well-sourced starting point for your own modelling, and confirm live pricing with the vendor before you commit budget.
Can I buy compute on OMC today? No. OMC is operating a public testnet. Mainnet — when the network can accept paying jobs and providers can earn — opens on 1 January 2027. You can join the testnet now and register for the community airdrop, but there is no compute to purchase and no price to pay.

### Model your own workload
The methodology behind OMC's delivered-cost comparisons, and the full billing design, are documented in the whitepaper.

Disclaimer: this calculator is an educational tool. Figures are third-party list prices observed in September 2026 and are provided without warranty; they are not an offer, a quotation or financial advice. OMC publishes no network rate and sells no compute today.

## Press Kit
Logos, boilerplate, share cards, and the source file behind every number on this site — so anything you publish about Omniverse Compute can be checked rather than trusted.
Updated 1 November 2026 · maintained by the project team

This page exists because most of what
gets written about a pre-launch token is copied from another article that copied it
from a listing site. Every figure below is generated from
contracts/params.json,
the file the contracts are deployed from, and republished machine-readable at
omc.network/airdrop.json. If you cite this page, you are
citing the source rather than a summary of it.

### Boilerplate
Three lengths, ready to paste. They say the same thing;
pick the one that fits the space.

#### One line · 24 words
Omniverse Compute is a decentralized GPU network on BNB Chain. Requesters pay for compute in OMC; node operators stake OMC, serve jobs, and earn an 8% protocol fee.

#### Short · 55 words
Omniverse Compute (OMC) is a decentralized compute network on BNB Smart Chain. GPU operators stake OMC and register hardware; requesters pay for AI compute jobs in OMC. The protocol charges 8% of settled job volume — half burned, 30% to staked nodes, 20% to the treasury. Supply is fixed at one billion; emission is gated by real fee revenue.

#### Full · 120 words
Omniverse Compute (OMC) is a decentralized compute network on BNB Smart Chain that matches GPU operators with the people who need compute. Operators stake OMC as collateral — a bond sized in dollars, not in tokens, so it keeps its weight when the price moves — register their hardware, and execute jobs. Requesters pay in OMC, with a 10% discount for paying in OMC rather than in stablecoins. The protocol takes 8% of settled volume: 50% burned, 30% to staked operators, 20% to the treasury. Total supply is fixed at 1,000,000,000 with no inflation parameter, and new issuance is capped by trailing 30-day fee revenue, so a network that earns nothing issues nothing. Mainnet and token generation are scheduled for 1 January 2027.

### Fast facts
Project | Omniverse Compute — a decentralized GPU compute network
Ticker | OMC · BEP-20 on BNB Smart Chain
Total supply | 1,000,000,000 OMC — fixed; no inflation parameter exists
Emission | 400,000,000 OMC over ten years from 1 January 2027, gated by trailing 30-day fee revenue. A further 100,000,000 is a DAO reserve locked until 2037.
Protocol fee | 8% of settled job volume, charged to the requester: 50% burned, 30% to staked node operators, 20% to the treasury
What a node does | Stakes OMC, registers hardware, executes compute jobs, proves completion, earns fees and emission
Airdrop | 20,000,000 OMC — 1,000,000 slots of 20 OMC. Free to join; first come, first served. Claiming opens 1 January 2027 with a 0.01 BNB processing charge per entry.
Mainnet / TGE | 1 January 2027 — scheduled, not shipped
Live today | Public testnet (chainId 97), node client, staking and compute-market contracts, airdrop registration
Not live | Mainnet, OMC token contract, third-party audit, exchange listing, token price. Any contract naming OMC today is fraudulent.

### Brand assets
Right-click to save, or click a card to download. Free to

### How to write about it without being wrong
A short list, offered because these are the errors that
show up most often in coverage of this category:

- It is a network, not a coin. OMC is the unit that settles work on it. The
interesting claim is the fee flow, not the ticker.
- BEP-20, not ERC-20. OMC is issued on BNB Smart Chain.
- There is no price. OMC is not listed anywhere and is not sold by the
project. Any figure quoted as "the OMC price" is invented.
- The airdrop is free to join. Three social actions and a wallet signature.
A separate 0.01 BNB per entry is charged at claim time, inside the claim
transaction — a processing charge, not a purchase, and not a discount on OMC.
- Say "testnet" when describing what runs today. Mainnet, the token contract,
the audit and any listing are scheduled for 1 January 2027 or later.
- Staking APR is a division, not a promise. It is annual emission divided by
total staked, capped at 100%, and it is zero until the network earns fees. Do not
quote an APR as a yield.

### Airdrop, stated correctly
20,000,000 OMC — 2% of supply — in 1,000,000 slots of
20 OMC each, first come first served. Registration is open now and free: follow, retweet
and comment, join Telegram, then connect a BNB Smart Chain wallet and register up to five
base entries (plus one per invited wallet that registers, up to five more). Claiming opens
with mainnet on 1 January 2027 and closes 31 March 2027; unclaimed slots return to the
protocol. Machine-readable terms:
/airdrop.json. Full announcement:
/news/omc-airdrop-is-open.

### Attributable statements
Two paragraphs that can be quoted directly and attributed
to the Omniverse Compute team. They are positions, not marketing lines.
"We priced the emission schedule against fee revenue rather
than against a calendar, because a schedule can only answer how fast a pool may be spent.
It cannot answer whether the network is earning anything while it spends. If there is no
revenue, there is no emission — a network that never finds demand simply never inflates."
"The airdrop is free and we say so on the page, in the
announcement and in the machine-readable feed. The 0.01 BNB per entry is a processing
charge at claim time and it is published before anyone connects a wallet, because the
alternative — a number discovered at the wallet prompt — is how airdrops earn a
reputation they never recover from."

### Corrections
If something here is wrong, it is wrong everywhere it was
generated from, so the fix happens once. Open an issue at
github.com/CBTdao/omc-network/issues
or message us on X; corrections are republished in
News with the date they were made. If a third-party listing disagrees
with this page, the listing is stale — the repository is the source.

## About & Contact
URL: https://omc.network/about · lang: en

About

## About & Contact
Who we are, what is live today, and how to reach us.

### What we are building
Omniverse Compute (OMC) is a decentralized GPU compute network. We aggregate idle and under-used GPU capacity — from independent node operators, small data centres and community hardware — and route it to workloads that need it: AI training and inference, rendering and scientific simulation.
The network is designed around an open marketplace where committed capacity supplies guaranteed availability, and open capacity sells the hours nobody reserved. That structure, and the pricing it produces, is documented in our whitepaper and tested publicly on our testnet.

### What is live today

- Public testnet on BNB Smart Chain — verified test contracts, published RPC endpoints and a node onboarding guide on the Testnet page.
- Whitepaper v3.0 — architecture, verification and slashing rules, matching engine and full tokenomics, on the Whitepaper page.
- Open-source repository — website and documentation sources under an MIT licence at github.com/CBTdao/omc-network.
- Community airdrop — participation is open now; claiming opens with mainnet on 1 January 2027 (2% of supply; registering is free, each entry costs a non-refundable 0.01 BNB at claim — 0.05 BNB for a base claim of five, 0.1 BNB at the ten-entry cap — and the money funds development and operations; each entry is delivered in full when you claim it, with no cliff and no vesting tail). Details on the Airdrop page.
- Companion sites — AITop for AI tool comparisons and the DCF forum for long-form compute research.
Mainnet and compute mining are planned after the testnet phase; the current roadmap is published on the News page and in the whitepaper.

### How we work
We publish the engineering roadmap and the repository in public, and we ship in small increments that anyone can verify. Where we make a factual claim about pricing, performance or market structure, we publish the methodology alongside it so it can be checked.

### Editorial standards
Our research and review content follows three rules, and we apply them to every piece we publish:

- No paid placements. Rankings and reviews are not sold, and no brand pays us for a position.
- No affiliate links. We do not earn commissions from the products we compare.
- Methodology in the open. Where we compare tools or rates, we state the criteria, the date and the sources.
We write about the crypto and AI industries, including projects we do not work with, and we publish critical conclusions about them when the evidence supports it.

### Contact

- Email: support@omc.network — for general questions, press and content corrections.
- X / Twitter: @Omniverse_Depin — project announcements.
- Telegram: t.me/OmniverseCompute — community chat.
- GitHub: CBTdao/omc-network — code, issues and contribution guide.
If you find an error in one of our articles, email us with the URL and the correction: we update the piece and note the change.

### Security notice
We will never ask for your seed phrase or private key, and we will never ask you to send BNB to an address we give you. Registering an entry is a free signature; the only money that ever moves is inside the claim transaction itself — the claim fee, 0.01 BNB per entry, plus network gas. The fee is not refunded (0.05 BNB for a five-entry claim), and it is a processing fee on the airdrop, not a price for the tokens: it is the same 0.01 BNB whether OMC trades at $0.01 or $1. Nobody from OMC will contact you first asking to "validate" or "unlock" a wallet. Treat any such message as an attempted scam, and report it to us at the email address above.

Legal

## Privacy Policy
Effective date: October 4, 2026 · Last updated: October 4, 2026

This Privacy Policy explains how the Omniverse Compute ("OMC") project team ("we", "us") collects, uses and protects information when you visit omc.network and its subdomains, including top.omc.network and forum.omc.network (together, the "Site").
This document is provided in English. It is the authoritative version of our privacy practices.

### 1. Summary

- We do not require an account, and we do not ask for your name, postal address or phone number.
- We do not run our own advertising or behavioural tracking pixels.
- We use browser localStorage — not cookies — to remember your language choice and your local airdrop activity record.
- Third-party advertising is served by Google AdSense, which may set cookies and use device identifiers. You control this through the consent message and Google's ad settings (see section 5).
- We never ask for your seed phrase or private key. Nobody from OMC will ever request them.

### 2. Information we collect
2.1 Information you give us. If you contact us by email or through our social channels, we receive the content of your message and your contact details. We use these only to answer you.
2.2 Wallet and blockchain data. The Airdrop page can connect a browser wallet (for example MetaMask) so that you can sign to prove address ownership. In that case we process your public wallet address and the signature. A public address and its on-chain history are inherently public information recorded on a blockchain. We never obtain, request or store your private key or seed phrase.
2.3 Automatically processed technical data. Our hosting provider processes standard server logs when you request a page — IP address, browser user agent, requested URL and timestamp — for security, abuse prevention and performance monitoring. These logs are retained by the provider for a short period.
2.4 Local storage on your device. We use localStorage keys for the following purposes. They stay on your device and are not transmitted to us:

- omc_lang — your selected interface language.
- omc_airdrop_v1 — your local record of airdrop entries.
- omc_session_v1 — a wallet session marker on the Airdrop page.

You can clear these at any time in your browser settings.

### 3. How we use information

- To operate, secure and improve the Site and the testnet.
- To let you participate in the community airdrop and to prevent abuse such as duplicate or automated claims.
- To display advertising that funds the project (see section 5).
- To respond to your enquiries.
- To comply with applicable legal obligations.
We do not sell your personal information.

### 4. Cookies and similar technologies
We do not set first-party cookies for analytics or profiling. Cookies and similar technologies on the Site come from third-party advertising (Google AdSense) and from embedded third-party content. Those third parties may collect information directly from your browser when their content is loaded or an ad is served.

### 5. Third-party advertising (Google AdSense) and personalized ads
The Site is monetized with Google AdSense. Google and its partners may use cookies, web beacons and device identifiers to serve ads based on your prior visits to this and other websites.

- Google's use of advertising cookies enables it and its partners to serve ads based on your visits to this Site and/or other sites on the internet.
- You may opt out of personalized advertising by visiting Google Ads Settings.
- You can also opt out of some third-party vendors' use of cookies for personalized advertising at aboutads.info and, in the EU/UK, at youronlinechoices.eu.
- For more information, see How Google uses information from sites that use its services and the Google Privacy Policy.
Where required by law (for example in the EEA, the UK and Switzerland), we present a consent message before advertising cookies are used, provided through Google's certified consent management platform. You can change or withdraw your consent at any time by using the privacy options link shown on the Site.

### 6. Third-party services we rely on

- Vercel — website hosting and delivery. Privacy policy
- Google AdSense — advertising. Privacy policy
- GitHub — source code hosting and, on our forum, the comment system (giscus), which stores your comments in GitHub Discussions. Privacy statement
- Telegram and X (Twitter) — community channels. If you open them, their own privacy policies apply.
- BNB Chain — public blockchain networks where our testnet contracts are deployed. On-chain data is public and outside our control.

### 7. Legal bases (EEA / UK)
Where the GDPR or UK GDPR applies, we process information on the following bases: your consent (advertising cookies and personalized ads), our legitimate interests (security, abuse prevention, operating the Site), the performance of a service you request (answering enquiries, enabling airdrop participation) and compliance with legal obligations.

### 8. Your rights
Depending on your location, you may have the right to: access the personal data we hold about you; request correction or deletion; restrict or object to processing; request data portability; withdraw consent at any time; and lodge a complaint with your local supervisory authority.
If you are a California resident, you have rights under the CCPA/CPRA to know what personal information is collected, to request deletion, to opt out of the "sale" or "sharing" of personal information, and to non-discrimination for exercising those rights. We do not sell personal information and we do not use your data for cross-context behavioural advertising other than through the advertising partners described in section 5, which is controlled by your consent choice.
To exercise any right, contact us at the address in section 13.

### 9. International transfers
The Site is served from global content-delivery infrastructure and our service providers may process information in countries other than yours, including the United States. Where required, transfers rely on appropriate safeguards such as standard contractual clauses offered by the relevant provider.

### 10. Data retention
We keep enquiry correspondence only as long as needed to respond and to keep records of the request. Server logs are retained by our hosting provider for a short operational period. On-chain data is permanent by design. Data in your browser's localStorage remains until you clear it.

### 11. Security
The Site is served over HTTPS. Because we hold very little personal data, we limit collection rather than rely on protection alone. No method of transmission or storage is completely secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security. You are responsible for the security of your own wallet and devices.

### 12. Children
The Site is not directed to children. We do not knowingly collect information from anyone under 16 (or the minimum age in your jurisdiction). If you believe a child has provided us with information, contact us and we will delete it.

### 13. Contact
Questions about this policy or requests relating to your data: support@omc.network. You can also reach us through the community channels listed on our About & Contact page.

### 14. Changes to this policy
We may update this policy to reflect changes in our practices or legal requirements. The effective date at the top of the page will always show the current version. Material changes will also be announced in the News section of the Site.

Nothing on the Site constitutes financial, investment, legal or tax advice, or an offer to sell securities. OMC is a utility token used within a decentralized computing network. Digital assets are highly volatile and carry the risk of total loss. Always do your own research and comply with the laws of your jurisdiction.

## Acceptable Use Policy
URL: https://omc.network/aup · lang: en

Acceptable Use Policy · v1.0

## Acceptable Use Policy
Rules for everyone who requests jobs or provides GPU capacity on the OMC network. Last updated: October 4, 2026.

Language. This policy is published in English; the English version is the authoritative reference. Report violations to security@omc.network.

### 1 · Scope
This Acceptable Use Policy ("AUP") governs all use of the OMC network: submitting compute jobs, providing GPU capacity, operating nodes, and interacting with the protocol's smart contracts. It applies to every participant, including those acting through automated systems. It supplements — and does not replace — the network's technical documentation and any terms shown in the product interface.

### 2 · Prohibited content
You may not submit, store, process or distribute content that:

- is illegal under the laws applicable to you or to the network's participants, including content that infringes intellectual property, privacy or data-protection rights;
- depicts or sexualizes minors, or constitutes child sexual abuse material in any form;
- promotes terrorism, violent extremism, targeted harassment, doxxing or credible threats of violence;
- constitutes malware, phishing kits, credential theft, or the distribution of viruses, ransomware or botnets;
- is designed to deceive: deepfakes of real people presented as authentic, forged documents, or fraud schemes.

### 3 · Prohibited workloads
You may not use OMC compute capacity to:

- mine proof-of-work cryptocurrencies other than through the protocol's own verified-job rewards;
- operate services whose purpose is denial-of-service, email or message spam, mass scanning, or password cracking against systems you do not own;
- bypass export controls or sanctions, or provide compute to persons or entities prohibited by applicable law;
- train or operate models for unlawful surveillance, unauthorized profiling of individuals, or weapons targeting;
- circumvent the network's verification, staking or payment mechanisms, including fake heartbeats, self-dealing jobs, or colluding nodes.

### 4 · Network integrity
Attacks on the network itself are prohibited: exploiting smart-contract bugs outside a disclosed and authorized bug-bounty program, Sybil attacks on rewards or airdrops, manipulation of reputation scores, interference with scheduling or settlement, and any attempt to steal staked funds or job escrow. Security research is welcome only under responsible disclosure through security@omc.network.

### 5 · Provider obligations
Providers must run the official node client unmodified in its verification-relevant parts, declare hardware attributes honestly (VRAM, interconnect, region, confidential-computing capability), keep staking requirements met, complete accepted jobs within the agreed limits, and wipe job data as required by the job's data-protection level. Providers are responsible for the physical and legal security of their own hardware.

### 6 · Requester obligations
Requesters must submit jobs they are legally entitled to run, hold the rights to the data and model weights they upload, respect the data-protection level they select, and pay from escrow as settled by the protocol. Requesters should not submit job types that the network has labeled as unverifiable if they require strong correctness guarantees.

### 7 · Enforcement
Violations may result in: immediate job termination without payment; slashing of staked OMC under the protocol's published rules; loss of reputation or node eligibility; and, where warranted, blacklisting of the account or node. Illegal activity may be reported to the competent authorities. Severe violations — in particular those in Section 2 — may result in permanent exclusion and forfeiture under the slashing rules applicable at the time.

### 8 · Reporting and appeals
Report violations, suspicious jobs or compromised nodes to security@omc.network, including job identifiers, timestamps and any supporting evidence. If your node or job was penalized and you believe this was an error, contact the same address with the job identifiers; disputes follow the process described in the whitepaper (Section 5).

### 9 · Changes
This AUP may be updated as the network develops. Material changes are announced on the News page before taking effect, and the version date at the top of this page is updated accordingly. Continued use of the network after a change takes effect constitutes acceptance of the updated policy.
Related documents. Privacy Policy · About & Contact · Whitepaper v3.0

## Compute for the Agent Economy
URL: https://omc.network/agent-economy · lang: en

Agent economy

## Compute for the Agent Economy
Always-on inference, machine-to-machine payment, and settlement per verified result.

Omniverse Compute (OMC) is building the settlement layer for the agent economy: autonomous software buys GPU time, pays for verified results, and settles machine-to-machine on BNB Chain. The unit of commerce moves from a reserved GPU hour to a completed, checkable inference — the only thing an agent actually consumes.

### From GPU hours to verified outcomes
Cloud pricing starts with a reservation: rent a box for an hour, keep the queue short, pay whether the job succeeds or not. An always-on agent has the opposite shape. It emits thousands of small requests, each with a result that can be checked, and it needs a price attached to that result rather than to the idle hardware around it.
OMC prices compute at the outcome. A requester escrows the job, a node runs it, and the release condition is the verifiable completion of that job. Matching, staking and settlement sit behind that one sentence — the commercial interface stays deliberately small: one request, one result, one settlement.

### Machine-to-machine payment is the default
Agents do not fill in billing forms. They need a credential, a meter and a way to top up without a human in the loop. OMC's tool endpoints use prepaid credits redeemed against an on-chain transfer: the service verifies the transaction on BNB Chain, debits one unit per completed job, and returns the unit when inference fails. The server holds no private key, and tool revenue is accounted for separately from every other flow in the project.
That pattern scales down to sub-cent requests and up to long-running agents that buy capacity continuously. It is also the shape on-chain settlement was built for: small, frequent, auditable transfers between two programs.

### Why inference, and why now
Training is episodic; inference is continuous. As agents move from demos into production, the demand curve stops resembling a quarterly batch job and starts resembling a utility bill. The bottleneck shifts from raw FLOPS to availability, verification and settlement latency — the three things a decentralized grid competes on.
Routing therefore treats verification as a dial. Spot-check re-execution suits batch work; redundant execution across independent nodes suits high-stakes results; hardware TEEs suit confidential workloads. Requesters choose the policy and pay for the assurance their job needs. The verifiable compute page describes the ladder.

### The parameters behind the model
Settlement layer | BNB Chain · chain ID 56
Token | BEP-20 · OMC · fixed supply
Billing unit | one verified result
Verification | requester-selectable: spot-check / redundancy / TEE
Payment | prepaid credits redeemed against an on-chain transfer
Off-chain signatures | ML-DSA (Dilithium, FIPS 204)
Roadmap | agent settlement → M2M metering → verifiable inference → post-quantum migration

### Questions

#### What does an agent actually pay for?
A completed result that passes the verification policy chosen for that job. Hardware time is an input to the node's own economics, not the line item on the requester's invoice.

#### Who holds the funds while a job runs?
The job fee sits in escrow and releases when the verifiable end state is reached. For metered tool traffic, prepaid credits are debited per completed call and returned when a call fails.

#### Where does this go next?
Agent-facing APIs, continuous metering, and a verification ladder priced by risk. Each stage is published on the news page and in the whitepaper.

## Verifiable Compute & Outcome-Based Billing
URL: https://omc.network/verifiable-compute · lang: en

Verifiable compute

## Verifiable Compute
Trust-minimized inference, priced per result, with a verification dial the requester controls.

Verifiable compute is decentralized GPU work whose completion can be checked before anyone gets paid. OMC makes that check a requester-controlled dial — spot-check re-execution, redundant execution across independent nodes, or a hardware trusted execution environment — and bills against the checked result instead of the reserved GPU hour.

### Escrow first, compute second
A requester locks the job fee in escrow before a node is dispatched. Release is tied to the job reaching a verifiable end state. The release condition lives in the contract rather than in an operator's promise, which removes the simplest failure mode: taking payment for work nobody did.
Escrow settles payment fraud. Correctness is a separate question, and that is where verification comes in.

### Verification is per job, not per network
There is no single switch that makes arbitrary computation trustworthy. The right policy depends on what the job is and what a wrong answer costs:

- Spot-check re-execution — re-run a random sample of batch work on a second node and compare output hashes. Catches silent errors and lazy nodes at a cost proportional to the check rate.
- Redundant execution — dispatch the same task to 2–3 independent nodes and accept consensus. The strongest option, reserved for results whose downside is expensive.
- Hardware TEE — prove the computation ran inside shielded hardware for confidential models and datasets, trading portability for confidentiality.
Treating verification as a dial rather than a flag is what makes outcome-based billing practical: every job carries the assurance it needs, and no job pays for assurance it does not need.

### Reputation is the slow signal
Escrow and verification settle one job. Reputation makes the next thousand cheaper. Nodes that complete work, pass checks and stay online accumulate standing; routing weights that standing together with TFLOPS, VRAM and bandwidth. The matching score is published in the whitepaper, and the tier ladder is live on the testnet.

### The parameters
Settlement | BNB Chain · chain ID 56 · escrow release on verifiable completion
Billing unit | one verified result
Verification ladder | spot-check / redundancy / hardware TEE
Routing inputs | TFLOPS, VRAM, bandwidth, reputation
Failure handling | metered tool calls return the debited credit
Off-chain signatures | ML-DSA (Dilithium, FIPS 204)

### Questions

#### Does every job need redundant execution?
No. Redundancy is the expensive end of the ladder. Batch preprocessing usually needs only sampling; a high-value result is where consensus earns its cost.

#### What happens when a node returns a plausible but wrong answer?
The chosen verification policy decides: sampling compares hashes, redundancy compares independent results, and failing a check keeps the escrow from releasing.

#### How is this priced?
Per verified result. The requester selects the verification policy, and that choice is part of the job's price. See compute for the agent economy for the settlement model.

## Post-Quantum Signature Migration
URL: https://omc.network/post-quantum · lang: en

Signature agility

## Post-Quantum Signature Migration
ML-DSA off chain today, signature agility in the contracts, and a migration path that follows the base layer.

OMC's post-quantum programme starts on the layers the project controls: service traffic signed by OMC already uses ML-DSA (Dilithium, FIPS 204), contracts keep signature agility, and the migration path follows BNB Chain as it adopts post-quantum signature standards. Custody on the base layer uses ECDSA / secp256k1 — the same assumption shared by every BSC asset — and the timeline is published as a roadmap.

### ML-DSA on the service layer
The ai-tools service and claim authorizations are the parts of the stack whose signature scheme OMC chooses itself. They use ML-DSA, the NIST FIPS 204 standard derived from Dilithium, with a working keygen / sign / verify implementation published in ai-tools-service/dilithium-poc. ML-DSA-65 keys and signatures are measured in that repository so the cost of the migration is visible rather than hypothetical.
Starting here has a practical advantage: the service layer ships on our schedule, while base-layer signature support moves on the chain's schedule. Both tracks advance in parallel.

### Signature agility in the contracts
Upgradeable contracts plus a verification interface that can accept new schemes are the mechanism that makes a later migration an orderly rollout. Privileged roles move to a 3-of-5 multisig with a 48-hour timelock before mainnet, and independent audits complete before launch — the same access-control work that governs every other upgrade.
The post-quantum roadmap tracks the standards work, the address-hygiene guidance and the migration stages in one place.

### Address hygiene and harvest-now-decrypt-later
Public keys become visible when an address is used. Guidance published for users covers address reuse, key rotation and the handling of long-lived authorizations, so the migration is a change of scheme rather than a scramble to clean up years of exposure.

### The parameters
Off-chain signatures | ML-DSA (Dilithium, FIPS 204)
Reference implementation | ai-tools-service/dilithium-poc · ML-DSA-65 / ML-DSA-87
Base-layer custody | BNB Chain · ECDSA / secp256k1
Contract model | upgradeable · multisig + 48-hour timelock before mainnet
Standards tracking | BNB Chain post-quantum migration work, NIST FIPS 203/204/205
User guidance | address hygiene, key rotation, long-lived authorizations

### Questions

#### Which parts of the stack use post-quantum signatures today?
Off-chain traffic signed by OMC: the ai-tools service and claim authorizations. The verification implementation and its measured key and signature sizes are in the public repository.

#### How does token custody migrate?
By following the base layer. Contracts are upgradeable, the verification interface accepts new schemes, and the rollout stages are published on the roadmap alongside the chain's own standards work.

#### What can a user do now?
Follow the address-hygiene guidance: avoid reuse, rotate keys where practical, and keep long-lived authorizations short. Those habits pay off regardless of which scheme the chain adopts.
